newsitem.title: LATVIA: Balts put brave face on Perry NATO rebuff.
newsitem.headline: Balts put brave face on Perry NATO rebuff.

text.p: Baltic countries put on a brave face on Friday after U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said openly for the first time what had only been whispered privately in the past: the Balts are not ready for NATO.

Just five years after they quit the former Soviet Union, the Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia are eager for NATO security promises to guarantee their independence after centuries of Russian domination.
But Perry said on Friday after a meeting of NATO defence ministers in the Norwegian town of Bergen that he did not think the Balts were ready yet to be NATO members.
He left them some hope by stressing the "not yet" aspect of his words and that they could one day be NATO members.
Latvian Foreign Minister Valdis Birkavs said that despite Perry's comments, his country would not give up its NATO aim.
"For the time being we are still working (to be in the first round)," Birkavs told Reuters in an interview.
"It means we continue to show our real intention and the real necessity to be in the first enlargement," he added.
The Balts are in Partnership for Peace (PfP), which offers training and technical help but no security pledges, and have troops in the NATO force in former Yugoslavia.

Diplomats have long said the Balts' chances of getting into a first round of NATO expansion were small given strong Russian objections. Moscow is against NATO expansion as a whole but is particularly sensitive about the Baltic states.
For 50 years they were packed with Soviet bases as part of Moscow's Western flank and still have large Russian minorities.
"If we are speaking about not being ready, it does not mean that we cannot be ready," Birkavs added.
"We have shown clearly our willingness to be integrated into NATO and together with the NATO countries we must achieve the stage of ability (to enter NATO)," he said.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Povilas Gylys said that his country would still try and be included in the alliance at the same time as other eastern European countries.

"Currently an opinion on a limited NATO expansion is quite influential but Lithuania thinks that all countries aspiring to become members of the...alliance have to be admitted at the same time," he told the domestic news agency ELTA.
A senior Lithuanian foreign ministry official said that if his country was not in the first round, NATO should provide a clear framework for those countries that remain outside.
"Unless we have clear perspectives and are on the road to NATO membership, the expansion of NATO will not provide the security that it wants to create," the Lithuanian official said.
An Estonian official echoed his Baltic colleagues, saying Tallinn also wanted NATO to give some political acknowledgement to countries that were not members now but were on the path.
